newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan war goes silent after failed strikes.
newsitem.headline: Afghan war goes silent after failed strikes.

text.p: Anti-Taleban forces paused on Monday after failing to dent the front lines of the purist Islamic militia or to damage its main air base.
Taleban fighters near the front lines some 25-30 km (15-19 miles) north of the Afghan capital said that by late afternoon barely a shot had been fired all day.
The pause followed the failure of the northern alliance trying to drive the Taleban out of Kabul to dislodge the militia defending a line of hills straggling across the plain north of the city.
Bombing raids by the small airforce of Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum for the second night running also failed to damage Kabul airport, used for both military and civilian traffic.
Airport sources said Dostum warplanes dropped three bombs inside the airport perimeter on Sunday night, but struck well away from the runway and warplanes sitting in taxi areas and caused no damage.
On Monday morning, two MiG-21s and a Sukhoi fighter-bomber were being readied to return to the battlefront and there were no signs they would be impeded.
Dostum, allied with former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, was apparently trying to stop the Taleban using Kabul airport to strengthen their front lines.
A Dostum bomber hit a city centre park on Saturday night, but injured no one.
The Taleban, who drove Masood from the capital a month ago, and Dostum forces sent warplanes into action on Sunday in the battle north of Kabul.
A Masood spokesman said late on Sunday the latest alliance bid to break through the Taleban lines had failed.
"We captured the high points which were planned," said Abdullah of the renewed attack on the De Sabz pass 30 km (19 miles) north of Kabul. "But the whole pass has not been secured."

Afghan watchers in Kabul say the alliance forces must punch through the hills to be able to push the Taleban back across the plain to the fringes of the Kabul valley and to break out of vulnerable positions on their side of the plain.
An alliance source admitted as much.
"We are exposed. It is a problem," the source told Reuters correspondent Chris Bird on the northern side of the front line.

"The alliance problem is that they're going to have to move forwards or backwards. They can't stay where they are for much longer or the Taleban are just going to sit back and pound them to pieces from long range," said one Afghan watcher with a military background.
"I expect they will try again. They have to break the stalemate," he said of the alliance.
The front line has been static for a week and the Taleban are clearly regaining confidence after being pushed back from Jabal os-Siraj by a counter-attack Masood launched just over two weeks ago.
The Afghan watcher said one strong sign of that confidence was a direct Taleban attack on Dostum in the far northwestern province of Badghis last week.
The Taleban say they have captured Badghis, pushed on into neighbouring Faryab province and were heading for its capital of Maimana, whose loss would be a very serious blow to Dostum.
There has been no independent account of the fighting in the remote region and Masood's spokesman Abdullah said on Saturday fighting was still going on in Badghis.
